code.title: Threads share the heap, each has its own stack

followUps:
On the heap, not on the stack. A lambda cannot keep a reference to a stack slot after the method returns, so the compiler copies the value into the lambda object, and that object lives on the heap.

This is why captured locals must be effectively final: the copy and the original could never diverge. If you need a changing value, capture an AtomicInteger or a one-element array; the object is shared, the reference is the copied part.

Usually about 512 KB to 1 MB per platform thread, depending on the platform. On 64-bit Linux the default is 1 MB (-Xss or -XX:ThreadStackSize changes it). That memory is reserved as virtual address space and only touched pages are really used.

Example: 1,000 threads reserve about 1 GB of address space, which is why thousands of platform threads get expensive and virtual threads (small, growable stacks on the heap) exist.

code.title: start() runs a new thread, run() does not

followUps:
It prints main. Calling run() directly is just an ordinary method call, so the body executes on the caller's thread, and Thread.currentThread().getName() inside it returns the caller's name, not "worker".

Only start() creates a new thread. Example: new Thread(task, "worker").run() from main prints "main"; with start() it prints "worker".

Use a Callable, which returns a value and may throw, and submit it to an executor. You get a Future; calling future.get() waits for the result.

ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
Future<Integer> f = ex.submit(() -> 6 * 7);
int v = f.get(); // 42
ex.shutdown();

A plain Runnable returns nothing, so the alternatives are shared fields (needs safe publication) or a join() plus a field.

code.title: Printing the six thread states

followUps:
TIMED_WAITING. The thread is parked for a fixed time and wakes by itself when the time is up (or earlier if interrupted). It keeps any monitors it already holds.

Example: a thread that calls Thread.sleep(500) shows TIMED_WAITING in getState() for about 500 ms, then returns to RUNNABLE.

Most likely they are RUNNABLE but not on a CPU: blocked in native I/O (a socket read, a file read, a database call). Java reports a thread inside a blocking native call as RUNNABLE even though the OS has it asleep.

Check a thread dump: look at the top frame. SocketInputStream.read or epollWait means waiting on the network, not computing. Low CPU plus many RUNNABLE threads usually means slow downstream calls.

code.title: synchronized makes a counter exact

followUps:
No. A static synchronized method locks the Class object, an instance synchronized method locks this. They are two different monitors, so both can run at the same time.

Example: thread A runs static synchronized foo(), thread B runs synchronized bar() on an instance: no blocking between them. If both touch the same static data, you must use the same lock for both.

Because strings can be interned: equal literals are the same object across the whole JVM. Your synchronized("lock") then shares a monitor with any unrelated library that also uses the literal "lock", so unrelated code blocks each other or even deadlocks.

Same problem for boxed Integer values (cached) and Boolean. Lock a private final Object that nobody else can reach.

code.title: volatile stop flag works, count++ does not need it

followUps:
No. volatile applies to the reference arr only. Writing arr[3] = 7 is a plain write to an element with no visibility guarantee.

Fixes: use AtomicIntegerArray or VarHandle element access, guard with a lock, or replace the whole array (copy, modify, then assign to the volatile field) so the volatile write publishes it.

It means read mostly under no lock, write under a lock. Readers read a volatile field, writers take a lock so only one writes at a time.

volatile int value;
synchronized void inc() { value++; } // one writer at a time
int get() { return value; }          // cheap read, always fresh

It is correct because the lock gives atomic updates and the volatile gives readers visibility. Reads are about as cheap as plain reads.

code.title: Happens-before: volatile flag publishes data

followUps:
DRF-SC: if a program has no data races, it behaves as if threads were simply interleaved one step at a time (sequential consistency). You can then ignore reordering and caches when reasoning.

So the practical rule is: protect every shared access with a lock, volatile or an atomic, and you can think in simple interleavings. Only racy code exposes weird reorderings.

• Initialize it in a static initializer.
  • Store it in a volatile field.
  • Store it in an AtomicReference.
  • Store it in a field guarded by a lock (and read under the same lock).
  • Make all its fields final (immutable) and the object not leak this from the constructor.

Handing it over via a concurrent collection (put then take) also works.

code.title: Double-checked locking with volatile, and the holder idiom

followUps:
To avoid reading a volatile field twice. A volatile read is cheaper than a lock but still costs more than a plain read. With a local, the common case (already initialized) does exactly one volatile read, then uses the local.

It also makes the code safe against the field changing between the check and the return. It is a small optimization, not needed for correctness.

Since Java 5, yes in principle: final fields are frozen at the end of the constructor, so a thread that sees the reference also sees the final fields' values, even if the reference was published through a race.

But it only covers the final fields. Any non-final field or anything reachable through non-final state may still look half-built. So it works for fully immutable classes only; otherwise use volatile.

code.title: wait/notifyAll in a while loop: simple hand-off

followUps:
A lost notification is a notify() that happens when nobody is waiting yet, so it is gone, and the thread that starts waiting afterwards sleeps forever.

The fix is to keep the condition in a variable (here full) checked under the same lock. A late waiter checks the flag first, sees it already true, and never waits at all. State, not the signal, is the truth.

Condition objects let one lock have several wait sets. A bounded buffer uses notFull and notEmpty, so a producer signals only consumers and the other way round.

With notifyAll every waiter wakes, even those that must go back to sleep: with 100 waiters that is 100 wake-ups for 1 useful. With conditions you can use signal() safely and wake exactly one waiter of the right kind.

code.title: Bounded buffer with synchronized, wait and notifyAll

followUps:
With if, a thread that wakes up does not re-check the condition and goes on even if it is false. Two bad cases: a spurious wake-up, or two consumers woken for one item, where the second finds the queue empty.

Example: if (q.isEmpty()) wait(); return q.removeFirst(); throws NoSuchElementException when the item was already taken. while checks again and waits again.

Use the timed wait with a deadline and keep the loop. Compute the deadline once so wake-ups do not extend the total wait.

long end = System.nanoTime() + nanos;
while (q.size() == capacity) {
  long left = end - System.nanoTime();
  if (left <= 0) return false; // timed out
  TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.timedWait(this, left);
}

BlockingQueue.offer(x, timeout, unit) does exactly this.

code.title: Deadlock-free transfer using lock ordering

followUps:
Lock both accounts in a fixed global order, here by id, so two transfers in opposite directions never wait on each other in a cycle.

Account lo = a.id < b.id ? a : b;
Account hi = lo == a ? b : a;
synchronized (lo) { synchronized (hi) {
  a.balance -= amt; b.balance += amt; } }

If ids can tie, break the tie with a global tie-lock or System.identityHashCode plus a fallback lock.

Tasks in a pool wait for other tasks that are stuck in the same pool queue, so no thread is free to run them. Nothing holds a lock; the threads are simply all taken.

Example: a pool of 2 threads, 2 tasks each submit a subtask to the same pool and call get(). Both threads block, the subtasks wait in the queue forever. Fix: use separate pools, a bigger or unbounded pool, or CompletableFuture chains instead of blocking.

code.title: Avoiding livelock: tryLock with random back-off

followUps:
A fair lock hands the lock to the longest waiter, so a woken thread must be scheduled before anything else can run. A normal lock lets the running thread grab it again right away (barging), which avoids a context switch.

Typical effect: fair locks give far lower throughput, often several times slower under contention, in return for predictable waiting. Use them only when starvation really occurs.

Same shape: many clients fail, retry immediately and together, so the retries themselves overload the service and cause more failures. Nobody makes progress while everyone is busy.

Fixes match: exponential back-off with random jitter (wait 100, 200, 400 ms plus random), a retry budget or circuit breaker, and limited retries. Without jitter, 1,000 clients retry at the same instant every time.

code.title: Race condition without a data race: check-then-act

followUps:
Check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);. Every call is thread-safe, but two threads can both see "absent" and both put, so one value is lost.

Fix with one atomic call: map.putIfAbsent(k, v) or computeIfAbsent. Same for map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1): use merge(k, 1, Integer::sum).

All threads that race compute the same value from the same immutable char[]. String.hashCode stores it in a plain int field, and the worst case is that two threads compute it twice and write the same number.

An int write is atomic, so no thread can see a torn value. The only unsafe reading is the default 0, which means "not computed yet", so it is just recomputed. A benign race, but it only works because of these exact facts.

Lightweight locking means locking with a quick compare-and-swap (CAS) on the object header, no OS call. Lock coarsening is when the JIT merges several adjacent lock/unlock pairs on the same object into one bigger critical section.

Example: a loop appending to a StringBuffer 1,000 times takes the lock 1,000 times; coarsened it takes it once. The harm is latency: the lock is held longer, so other threads wait longer. A coarse lock over slow work (I/O) hurts tail latency.

Record the JFR event jdk.JavaMonitorEnter, which logs each time a thread had to wait to enter a monitor, with duration and the class of the monitor.

Steps: start with jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr, open it in JDK Mission Control or run jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter rec.jfr, then sort by total blocked time. Take thread dumps to confirm which stack holds the lock.

A volatile read compiles to a load-acquire instruction, ldar, and a volatile write to a store-release, stlr. These keep the right ordering without a full barrier: nothing after an ldar can move before it, and nothing before an stlr can move after it.

Plain loads (ldr) and stores (str) have no such guarantee, which is why a non-volatile flag can fail on ARM but seem fine on x86.

When you need only part of what volatile gives, or element-level access. Acquire/release orders just enough for hand-offs (a flag publishing data), and is cheaper on ARM than the full sequential consistency of volatile. Opaque mode is for counters and flags where order does not matter.

VarHandle also gives volatile access to array elements and CAS on fields. It is harder to get right, so use it only after measuring, for example in lock-free queues.

code.title: Stopping a thread with interrupt, restoring the flag

followUps:
Because the exception is the signal. Once the thread has been told, the flag is reset to false so the thread is back to a normal state and can continue (or throw on). The information now lives in the exception.

If you catch it and do not rethrow, the signal is lost. So either propagate it, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to set the flag again for callers up the stack.

You cannot interrupt a blocked socket read through interrupt(). Instead, close the socket from another thread: the blocked read then throws a SocketException and the worker exits.

Better options: set a read timeout (setSoTimeout) and check a stop flag after each timeout, or use NIO channels (InterruptibleChannel), where interrupt closes the channel and throws ClosedByInterruptException.
